content:
You can learn a lot by asking people who live in the area what already helps, and where help is still missing. A short survey can start that listening. It cannot finish it.

Use the answers to plan more conversations and, where it fits, a service partnership with people already doing the work. Do not use them to vote on doctrine, values, or the ministry approach you have already committed to.

---

## Start with help and existing strengths

Write the purpose in one sentence before you write a question. You are asking residents what helps their community and where help is missing. You are also asking who is already doing that work.

That second question is the one plants skip. A needs list, on its own, pushes a team to promise a program it cannot staff. It can also hide the school, clinic, association, or neighbor who has been at the work for years. The Asset-Based Community Development Institute treats local assets, not deficits, as the building blocks of community life. It names residents, associations, local institutions, the physical environment, the local economy, and local culture. Ask about those in your own area. Do not treat a block as empty because your team has not met the people yet.

<Callout type="insight">
A survey is a way to hear what residents already see. It is not a ballot on what the church should believe or do.
</Callout>

Keep the form short enough to finish at a door or a table. Hear open answers before you offer a list. People choose an offered option more often than they volunteer it.

---

## Write questions that do not lead

Ambiguous or biased questions waste the work of finding respondents. Small wording changes can change the answers. So can order. If you ask about your ideas first, people are more likely to echo them in the open question that follows.

Ask one thing at a time. "Is housing expensive and unsafe here?" forces one answer onto two problems. Use plain words. If a resident has to ask what you meant, the question is not ready.

Skip agree-disagree lines such as "This neighborhood needs a church-run youth program." Some people, especially those with less formal education, are more likely to agree with a statement than to choose between alternatives. That pattern is stronger when an interviewer is present. Ask an open question, or offer a real choice.

| Leading question | Clearer question |
|---|---|
| Don't you agree this area needs a church food pantry? | Where do people get food help now, and what is still missing? |
| Would you support our after-school program? | What already helps children after school, and where is help missing? |
| Is the neighborhood unsafe and neglected? | What feels unsafe here? What is already being done about it? |

Put open questions before any list your team already likes. If you use a closed list, add "something else" and a blank line. On a paper or online form, people tend to pick items near the top. In a telephone survey, they more often pick items they heard later. If you do not rotate the order, say so, and do not treat position as a stronger finding.

Pretest the form with a few residents who will tell you when a question is confusing or pushy. Change the wording before you print a stack.

<Callout type="tip">
Read each question aloud and ask what answer it is fishing for. If you can name that answer, rewrite the question.
</Callout>

---

## Tell people what you are collecting

Before the first question, say who is asking, what the answers will be used for, and that a person may skip any question or stop. If you do not need a name, do not ask for one.

Do not collect health details, income, immigration status, or information about children unless you have a clear reason and a way to keep those answers from spreading. Listening is not a reason to build a file on neighbors.

If you might quote a story, ask first, and remove details that point to a household. Store forms where only the people writing the summary can read them. Do not paste raw answers into a group chat.

People more often give a socially liked answer when an interviewer is present than when they fill out a form themselves. They may overstate church attendance and charitable intent. Answers given at a door, with a church member standing there, are polite conversation. They are not a measure of spiritual health.

<Callout type="warning">
Do not promise a program, a timeline, or a partnership to get a completed form. Thank the person and say you are listening. That is the commitment you can keep today.
</Callout>

---

## Say who answered, and who did not

Forms from one festival, one language, or one circle of friends are not the neighborhood. A nonprobability survey has no random selection from the whole population. If the people who answered differ from the people who did not, their views may not represent the area.

You do not need a probability sample to listen well. You do need to say who showed up. Most plants will hear from whoever stopped, opened the door, or already knows someone on the team. Do not use this form to pick a service time, a language, or a meeting format. Keep those questions for people who have agreed to help plant the church.

Write these down before you summarize.

- The area you meant, with the same boundaries as your map or demographic brief.
- The dates, the language, and how you asked. Door, event, paper, or online.
- Who was invited, as far as you know, and how many forms came back.
- Who is missing. A language you did not offer, blocks you never walked, or people who were at work when you asked.

Report figures as "of the people who answered," not "the community believes." Do not turn a small stack of forms into a percentage of the city, and do not assign a Census average to the people who filled out your form.

If you ask again later, keep the same wording and a similar place in the form. Otherwise you are asking a new question.

---

## Separate what you heard from what you conclude

Write the summary so another leader can tell a finding from a guess.

**What people said.** Themes, with a count of forms, next to the number of forms you had. A theme without a count is a story you liked. Quote a sentence only with permission, and only if it does not identify the speaker.

**What you did not hear.** Questions people skipped. Blocks with no forms. Topics nobody raised. Leave the gap empty. Do not fill it with the answer your team hoped to hear.

**What you will ask next.** Name conversations, not a program. Talk with the people already doing the work before you discuss any new effort of your own.

<Callout type="important">
Survey results do not set doctrine, values, or ministry priorities by vote. They are not a readiness condition for any phase. They do not measure spiritual health. Everyfield does not score a survey or certify a plant from one.
</Callout>

---

## Take the findings back into conversations

Use the summary to choose a few listening conversations, not a launch plan. A toolkit from the Institute of Museum and Library Services describes a listening campaign as learning conversations over a longer stretch, used with asset mapping. You do not have to copy that format. Talk with the people and groups the forms named.

Ask what they are already doing, and what help they do not want. A partnership that adds work to their week is not help. A plant that arrives with a finished program has skipped the reason for the survey.

Only then consider a service partnership. Match it to people, time, and money you can spare without setting aside Worship, Walk, Work, and Witness. If you cannot staff the help through a season, do not announce it. Offer something smaller, or keep listening.

The Senior Pastor and the other leaders still hold the church's doctrine, values, and ministry approach. Residents can show you a need and a neighbor. Their preferences do not replace those commitments.

- [ ] State what helps, what is missing, and who is already at work.
- [ ] Pretest the form and drop any question that leads.
- [ ] Say who is asking, how answers will be used, and that people may skip or stop.
- [ ] Record who was invited, who answered, and who is missing.
- [ ] Separate findings from the questions you still have.
- [ ] Talk with people already doing the work before you offer a partnership.
- [ ] Promise only what the plant can deliver.

<Callout type="scripture">
*"‘Seek the peace of the city where I have sent you into exile, and pray to Yahweh on its behalf; for in its peace you will have peace.’"* — Jeremiah 29:7 (LSB)
</Callout>

Seeking the peace of the place is why you ask. The form is only one way to listen.
excerpt: Ask residents what already helps and where help is missing. Report who answered, and use the results for listening, not a vote.
title: Running a Community Needs Survey

sources.claim: Ambiguous or biased questions undermine a survey even if the sample is otherwise sound, and small wording differences can change answers.
sources.quote: Accurate random sampling will be wasted if the information gathered is built on a shaky foundation of ambiguous or biased questions.

sources.claim: Small differences in question wording can substantially change the answers people give.
sources.quote: Even small wording differences can substantially affect the answers people provide.

sources.claim: Offering an answer in a closed list increases how often people choose it, compared with an open question where they must volunteer it.
sources.quote: When explicitly offered the economy as a response, more than half of respondents (58%) chose this answer; only 35% of those who responded to the open-ended version volunteered the economy.

sources.claim: Questions that combine two ideas are hard to answer and hard to interpret.
sources.quote: Questions that ask respondents to evaluate more than one concept (known as double-barreled questions) – such as “How much confidence do you have in President Obama to handle domestic and foreign policy?” – are difficult for respondents to answer and often lead to responses that are difficult to interpret.

sources.claim: Some respondents, especially those with less formal education, are more likely to agree with a statement than to choose between alternatives.
sources.quote: Research has shown that, compared with the better educated and better informed, less educated and less informed respondents have a greater tendency to agree with such statements.

sources.claim: Pretesting is an essential step when questions are new.
sources.quote: Pretesting a survey is an essential step in the questionnaire design process to evaluate how people respond to the overall questionnaire and specific questions, especially when questions are being introduced for the first time.

sources.claim: Earlier questions can shape answers to later open questions, so open questions belong before related closed lists.
sources.quote: If closed-ended questions that relate to the topic are placed before the open-ended question, respondents are much more likely to mention concepts or considerations raised in those earlier questions when responding to the open-ended question.

sources.claim: On self-administered forms people tend to choose items near the top. In telephone surveys they more often choose items heard later.
sources.quote: Research suggests that in telephone surveys respondents more frequently choose items heard later in a list (a “recency effect”), and in self-administered surveys, they tend to choose items at the top of the list (a “primacy” effect).

sources.claim: Social desirability bias is greater with an interviewer present. People may overstate church attendance and charitable contributions.
sources.quote: They also may overstate church attendance, charitable contributions and the likelihood that they will vote in an election.

sources.claim: Comparing results over time requires the same question wording.
sources.quote: When measuring change over time, it is important to use the same question wording and to be sensitive to where the question is asked in the questionnaire to maintain a similar context as when the question was asked previously

sources.claim: A nonprobability survey has no random selection from the whole population, so the answers may not represent that population.
sources.quote: With non-probability polls, there's no random selection from the entire population. Meaning that researchers don't know the chance - or probability - that each person has of being selected for any given poll.

sources.claim: If survey respondents differ from the broader population, their views may not represent it.
sources.quote: So if the people in the surveys are different from the broader population, their views may not be representative of the entire population.

sources.claim: Asset-based community development starts from local assets, including residents, associations, institutions, the physical environment, the local economy, and local culture, rather than treating neighborhoods as only deficits.
sources.quote: ABCDI considers local assets of individuals, associations, local institutions, the physical environment, the local economy and local culture the primary building blocks of sustainable community development

sources.claim: The ABCD Institute treats assets and strengths, not deficits and needs, as the building blocks of healthy communities.
sources.quote: Assets and strengths, not deficits and needs, are the true building blocks of healthy communities.

sources.claim: A listening campaign is a longer process of learning conversations, used alongside asset mapping, not a single form.
sources.publisher: Institute of Museum and Library Services
sources.quote: A Listening Campaign is a more prolonged, 6- to 8-week process. It incorporates learning conversations, a classic organizing tool, alongside the agency-led asset-mapping tool.

sources.claim: The tendency to agree with a statement is stronger when an interviewer is present than when people fill out the survey themselves.
sources.quote: This behavior is even more pronounced when there’s an interviewer present, rather than when the survey is self-administered.

sources.claim: Social desirability bias is greater when an interviewer is present than when people complete the survey themselves.
sources.quote: Research has also shown that social desirability bias can be greater when an interviewer is present (e.g., telephone and face-to-face surveys) than when respondents complete the survey themselves (e.g., paper and web surveys).

claim_check.notes: Owner review by Sebastian; no model review per his 2026-10-26 instruction.

rulings: Bryan ruled B4 = Option A: "Find needs and existing strengths" (2026-10-26).

Wording call: this article does not teach Option B. It does not use survey answers to choose service times, languages, or meeting formats. Those questions stay with people who have agreed to help plant the church.
Wording call: no survey vendor, software platform, or ABCD Institute membership is recommended.
Wording call: consent and privacy steps are practical instructions, not a claim about a statute, an IRB rule, or a legal exemption. If a school or funder is involved, ask that body what it requires.

Wording call: Jeremiah 29:7 (LSB) is used for the motive of seeking the city's peace, not as a method for questionnaire design. The opening quotation mark is the carry mark printed in that verse on read.lsbible.org.
